newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia market watchdog hailed, gaps to be filled.
newsitem.headline: Croatia market watchdog hailed, gaps to be filled.

text.p: Market watchers and foreign investors on Tuesday welcomed the establishment of Croatia's securities watchdog but said authorities must fill remaining market gaps to improve stocks trading.

"The commission is a very important part of infrastructure, this is a positive step," Milan Elezovic at London's Nomura Research Institute told Reuters. "But other issues, including custodianship, remain unclear."

Three of five planned commissioners were named by the Croatian parliament at the weekend, raising hopes among market participants that at least some of their woes, including licensing of new brokers, would be resolved before long.

Although they said all appointed members were able, analysts voiced doubts as to how soon the short-staffed commission could become fully operational and what other key issues would fall under its competence.
"Assume only you and I were put in charge of a nuclear plant. There's not much we could do with it," one source said, adding it might be months before the new body asserts itself.
The commission should approve the opening of investment funds, which are seen as fundamental to the success of mass voucher privatisation planned for some time this winter.
It also must take over some Zagreb bourse responsibilities, such as supervision, which have so far been enforced only to some extent to appease wary portfolio investors.
Analysts said trading supervision should be stricter to prevent price rigging and other manipulations on a rapidly expanding Croatian market.
"We definitely need a helping hand," said Zeljko Kardum, spokesman for the Zagreb Stock Exchange.
He added that the commission would also have to push for the establishment of a central register for securities.

For now the transfer of shares to new owners is left to each company, which keeps an individual register. This often drags out the procedure and discourages potential investors in attractive, fast-earning local stocks.
Improving transparency is essential if Croatia wants to lure more big foreign buyers, market analysts warn.
"Better transparency will increase the market's potential and result in more activities by foreign investors," said Ratko Bajakic of Investmentbank Austria in Zagreb.

He added that settlement, which now takes up to seven days from each deal, could be speeded up to enable more efficient trading. "This is not a problem for a relatively slow market but a good target for the future could be T+3 (three days)." -- Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
